title: Horn
reference_instrument: University of Iowa MIS French horn (model unstated; performer J. Wiskus)
summary: A stand-in, and mostly not graded: a natural baroque horn in D on a trombone's artificial lip, with no hand in the bell and no valve tubing, beside Iowa's modern horn. A2 scores 5 of 11; A3 and D4 have no count, Db2 has no recording and Db5 doesn't speak. The baroque D4 takes about 1.9 s to come up. The bore is the plotted profile of Fig. 7 of Bilbao and Chick (2013, JASA 134), which the authors hand-measured to within 5 %: 114 vertices read from the figure's vector data, 4.52 m with the PHC 22 mouthpiece inside the bore, 111 cones on the card. The lip, the 6.22 kPa hold and the microphone are the tenor trombone's (Cullen 2000 Table A.2 embouchure 19, artificial latex lips on a trombone-size mouthpiece, not a horn player's). Every note now blows flat from rest, with no borrowed attack. A3 and D4 sit on the printed D crook (lip settings 0.80 and 1.10, picked from a nine-setting ladder by which bore peak each plays, no recording involved) and are posted for hearing. A2 and Db2 are on crooks of this model's own arithmetic on that bore, 0.138 m and 0.042 m shorter, solved once from the pitch a first try sounded (52 c and 100 c sharp); they now sound within about 3 c of equal temperament. A second card, a modern Bb horn with its valves open, adds four notes posted for hearing and with no count (slots F3-bbhorn, Bb3-bbhorn, D4-bbhorn and F4-bbhorn): its bore is the 'Bb Schmid' curve of Kemp, Chick, Campbell and Hendrie (2008, acoustic pulse reflectometry of an Engelbert Schmid double horn) read from two raster figures (148 stations to 98.75 mm at 2.77 m); the last 85 mm to the rim are the outer profile of a Kruspe double horn read from two Metropolitan Museum photographs (another horn's bell, image-read); the mouthpiece is the Paxman 3A of another horn; the lip, the 6.22 kPa hold and the microphone are the trombone card's again, with no hand in the bell and no valve tubing. Each note's lip pre-stress is the steady setting nearest equal temperament, never a pitch input, and each note reaches 90 % of its level in 0.31 to 0.49 s. The Iowa clip beside each of these pages is ff (F3, Bb3) or mf (D4, F4); the site's screen lists all four INVALID (snr and pitch), so nothing is graded. The card's passive impedance maxima lie 90 to 142 cents below the maxima measured on the Bb side of a Conn 8D horn (Watts 2009), a check and not an input.
physics_present: the generic lip-valve performer, outlet observer and file format used for the tenor trombone, now carrying a whole horn bore as cones: the passive plane-wave maxima of the digitised bore are 64.6, 102.9, 144.3, 181.2, 219.4 and 254.3 Hz against the authors' measured 64.8, 103.7, 144.7, 181.9, 220.3 and 256.2 Hz (all within 13 c)

a flat blow on all four notes: the pressure rises to 6.22 kPa in 0.05 s and stays, with the 12 kPa attack borrowed from the trombone removed, and each note settles on the hold the attack led to (same lip gap and closed share, pitch within 2 c)

flow noise at the lips on all four notes (Oldham and Ukpoho 1990, extrapolated), sized by the blowing pressure and the card's 9.014 mm rim radius with no level set: it brings the held note's harmonic-to-noise ratio near the recording's on A2 and most of the way on A3 and D4, but its floor has no frequency shape, so above 2 kHz it sits 3 to 35 dB over the recording's and the spectral distance doesn't improve

the lip's flow-area exponent as a trombonist's lips measured it, per note, ADDED to cards that carried none (the opening was the plain w h): Bromage, Campbell and Gilbert (2010, preprint HAL hal-00474644v1, Table 2; one trombonist, AJ, mezzo forte, high-speed video; 1.2 at Bb1, 1.3 at Bb2, 1.6 at F3, 1.9 at F4), by linear interpolation in MIDI between the printed notes and no extrapolation: q = 1.700 on A3 and 1.825 on D4, a trombonist's lips on a trombone mouthpiece and not a horn player's (a larger borrowing than the tuba's); a LARGE change, the opening growing by a factor of 2.0 to 3.7 on A3 and 1.7 to 3.4 on D4 at the new clips' own lip gaps; the held note moved +1.65 cents and +2.11 cents, the level of the held note rose 1.45 and 1.77 times and the band energy at 2 to 3 kHz 14.9 and 19.1 dB, and neither page has a count (both are posted under the rule that the page still speaks its note); the same row on A2 (q 1.292) made the count fall from 5 to 2 of 11 (harmonic levels, partial trajectories and attack left their rulers) and on Db2 (q 1.225) stopped the oscillation (the lip opens to a steady 2.919 mm and the level of the held note is 0.034 of the live clip's), so A2 and Db2 keep their previous clips

a modern Bb horn card, valves open (the Bb pages F3, Bb3, D4 and F4): 166 cones, 2.9107 m from the cup rim to the bell rim, the Schmid bore read from two raster figures, another horn's bell end and mouthpiece; the engine's passive maxima are 42.63, 114.62, 169.97, 229.55, 286.90, 343.47, 400.58 and 456.19 Hz; each note locks on the maximum of its own pitch, 24.5 to 44.5 cents above it, at lip settings 0.68 (F3, 174.40 Hz), 0.86 (Bb3, 232.83 Hz), 1.14 (D4, 293.71 Hz) and 1.34 (F4, 349.34 Hz), which sit -2.2, -1.9, +0.2 and +0.6 cents from equal temperament; each holds one partial for 4 s
physics_missing: the Iowa horn's own bore: no numeric table of a modern single or double horn's profile was found (the Bb pages read the Schmid double horn's profile from two raster figures of Kemp et al. 2008, and the Iowa horn is of a model the Iowa pages do not state); the Edinburgh museum catalogue lists about seven bore diameters at key points of one double horn, and the horn that speaks on the older pages is a different instrument (a baroque natural horn), read from a figure; the measured modern instrument that exists in print is a few numbers and not a profile: the Alexander (Mainz) full double horn in F with a Bb fourth valve of the Edinburgh University Collection (MIMEd record 15417, accession 1804, bore measured by A. Myers: sounding length 2635 mm in Bb, segment lengths 143, 551 and 873 mm, bell diameter 311 mm, bore 7.7 mm at its minimum, 11.3 mm at the main tuning slide, 11.9 mm at the valve tuning slide, 11.9 mm at 1418 mm from the bell end, 16.8 mm at about 835 mm and 114 mm at 74.5 mm from the bell end, mouthpiece receiver 8.7 mm; units not printed and read as millimetres; the bell flare field is empty), so only three diameters come with a position and a bore built from them would be invented between the points: no page is built from them (the Bb pages use the Schmid profile instead); two more measured double horns in the catalogue (John Grey and Sons, record 16565; Lidl, Brno, record 18259) carry fewer numbers; the Yamaha patent US 5,367,938 prints part lengths of 60, 500, 800, 550 and 850 mm and a constant valve-section diameter of 12.8 to 13.5 mm (the prior art 11.9 to 12.1 mm) and no other diameter; the Alexander's profile figure is in Campbell et al. (2004, Musical Instruments, OUP, p. 171, Fig. 5.10a), a book that was not open

the hand in the bell, which lowers the cutoff and moves the upper resonances on every note (Dell et al. 2015): that paper was not found. The same authors' ISMA 2010 paper (Dell, James, Davidson and Wolfe) prints measured input impedance of a modern Yamaha double horn with casts of three players' hands in the bell, with no hand and with four practice mutes (between the hands the rms difference of the impedance peaks 1 to 20 is up to 0.8 dB in magnitude and 0.6 Hz in frequency); it has none for a baroque horn, and no hand geometry is printed for any horn. That impedance is a check on a future hand model and not a target

rotor and branch-slide tubing for the F and B-flat sides, and a horn mouthpiece measured separately (the baroque card's PHC 22 cup is the first 63 mm of its measured bore, with the lumped cup volume at the format floor); a modern horn mouthpiece measured separately IS printed: the Paxman '3A' formerly used with the Alexander double horn above (Edinburgh record 16358: cup diameter 16.6 mm, throat 4.5 mm, cup depth about 26 mm, shank depth 31.7 mm, taper from 9.1 to 7.5 mm) and the maker's data for the Marcinkiewicz No. 7 that Dell et al. (ISMA 2010) used on a Yamaha 668 double horn (inside cup diameter 17.75 mm, cup depth 24.51 mm, throat 5.11 mm, length 63.50 mm), none with a backbore profile, and the baroque bore keeps its own PHC 22 while the Bb pages use the Paxman 3A, one cone each for cup and backbore between the printed ends; the only valve-tubing number printed is the Alexander's sounding length of 2635 mm in Bb, with no loop lengths

a lip valve for horn players: the lip is the trombone's artificial one, and on the low notes it swings far outside the opening it was measured at (maximum gap 5.6 to 6.5 mm at A2 and 18 mm at Db2, against a 9 mm wide lip and 1.5 mm at A3) A rim stop on the lip was tried at Db2 and moves the note: the opt-in card row lip_rim_stop (the lip gap may not exceed the first bore cone's diameter, 18.028 mm, and at that bound the lip's outward momentum is removed or reversed; no source measures that restitution) is on no posted page. On the binary that carries it the unchanged G3 card and the unchanged Db2 card each wrote their live clip byte for byte, and a stop set far above the swing steps the original operations bit for bit in the unit tests. With the stop the Db2 held note moved +73 c (inelastic) and +104 c (elastic) and the level +6.6 and +6.7 dB, from a stop that acted on 215 and 137 of 76800 samples, while the largest steady opening stayed 162.3 mm2; no recording exists at Db2 to say which render is nearer. The cause was read with a diagnostic bound of 19.0 mm, which is not the mouthpiece's geometry and lies 1 mm above the steady peak: the held note moved +69.8 c and the level +6.5 dB with 215 hits, within 3.3 c and 0.13 dB of the stop at 18.028 mm, so the move is not a trim of the steady peak. The start-up excursion is removed in every run and the lip then settles on a different branch with the stop acting every cycle; each hit removed 16.4 mJ, 46 % of the swing's spring-energy scale 0.5 k A^2 (the sum was 3.52 J), and about 95 % of that is the kinetic energy of the outward momentum that the inelastic stop zeroes (estimated from the sum, which the receipt carries as one number), so the energy goes out through the velocity zeroing and not through the position clamp. The elastic stop was not repeated with this accounting.

the pitch the lip settles on: on every steady note the sound is 2.0 to 4.5 Hz above the calculated bore maximum (13 to 30 c at A3 to E4); the engine's own passive maxima agree with a plane-wave sum to 0.6 Hz or better, so it isn't the bore calculation, and the peak's half-width doesn't explain it; the cause is not found; on the Bb pages the held notes sit 24.5 to 44.5 c above the passive maxima (F3 +44.5, Bb3 +24.5, D4 +40.6 and F4 +29.3 c), the same lock, equally unexplained

a Db5 that speaks: five lip settings from 0.84 to 0.96 of the calculated maximum start no oscillation at the trombone's 6.22 kPa hold or at 12 kPa, the old card's attack pressure; those settings make the lip 6 to 8 times stiffer than at A3, so a higher pressure is untried

a player's start to the note on the baroque pages: from rest on the flat blow A2 is up by about 0.4 s, A3 reaches 90 % of its level by 0.73 s, Db2 speaks from about 1.0 s and D4 is near silent until about 1.5 s, full by 1.9 s; the clips keep those leads
the dips at H3, H5, H8 and H10 on A2, which the recording doesn't have: they're already in the lip's flow, and why the lip makes them hasn't been traced

A player's tract upstream of the lip (opt-in, fs-couple brass_loop): the digitized LOW tract of one trumpeter (Kaburagi, Yamada, Fukui and Minamiya 2011, Fig. 3, Eb4, 311 Hz; section 0 removed, with the yielding wall of the voice cards) was tried as a declared stand-in on A3 (220.0 Hz) and D4 (293.66 Hz), the measured pitch lying 91 and 17.3 Hz above them, another player's tract on another instrument. Both renders were refused by the airway at the pages' 19200 Hz before any sound (the converged characteristic line violates 4x-oversampled passivity), while the same tract and wall passed at 48000 Hz on the trumpet Bb3 page. No horn player's tract was found, no tract value was adjusted, and both horn pages keep their cards; the two cards are to be re-run unchanged when the airway's rung climb for this refusal lands.

the Schmid horn's own bell and a measured mouthpiece contour: the last 85 mm of the Bb pages' bell (96.9 to 314.3 mm) are another horn's outer profile (Kruspe, Metropolitan Museum 503607) read from two photographs, with the scale resting on one stated number (the stated height does not fit at it), and the mouthpiece is the Paxman 3A of another horn; no picture or scan of the Schmid bell was found, the profile above about 60 mm diameter (x about 2.66 m) is outside the range in which plane-wave reflectometry is reliable, and the authors of the reflectometry paper have not been asked for their numeric profile (the owner's decision)

the Bb bore's pitch: the card's passive maxima (114.62, 169.97, 229.55, 286.90, 343.47, 400.58 and 456.19 Hz) lie 90 to 142 cents below those measured on the open Bb side of a Conn 8D (Watts 2009, a course report: 121.5, 184.5, 244.5, 302.5, 364.5, 425.5 and 480.5 Hz, read from the table's image, no hand): another horn and mouthpiece, the laboratory's air against the card's 27 C breath gas, and the reflectometer's reference plane are untried; the cause is not found, and the notes posted are the lip settings nearest equal temperament on this bore, not tuned to anything
a horn player's blowing pressure: the Bb cards blow the trombone's flat 6.22 kPa on every note while the Iowa clips are ff or mf; no horn-player pressure is on them yet
valve loops for the Bb pages: they play the open Bb series only, no loop length is printed for the Schmid and no valved note is claimed
blocked: No horn player's lip and no hand-in-bell geometry found in open literature; the older pages' bore is a baroque horn's (Bilbao and Chick 2013) and the Bb pages' bore is a modern horn's read from raster figures (the authors' table was not found), with another horn's bell end and mouthpiece.
